ch32.title: The Day the Five Thousand Were Fed
ch32.b002: The story of the cure of Amos, the Kheresa lunatic, had crossed the lake ahead of the boat, and a great crowd was waiting when Jesus landed that Tuesday forenoon. Among them were new observers from the Jerusalem Sanhedrin, come to find cause for the Master’s arrest. As Jesus greeted the people, Jairus, one of the rulers of the synagogue, pushed through the throng, fell at his feet, and took him by the hand: “⟦Q 152:0.1⟧Master, my little daughter, an only child, lies in my home at the point of death. I pray that you will come and heal her.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said: “I will go with you.”
ch32.b003: The crowd followed to see what would happen. Shortly before they reached the ruler’s house, as they hurried through a narrow street with the throng jostling him, Jesus suddenly stopped. “Someone touched me.” Those nearest denied it, and Peter protested that the crowd was pressing on every side. “I asked who touched me,” Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:0.2⟧for I perceived that living energy had gone forth from me.⟦/Q⟧” His eyes fell on a woman nearby, who came forward and knelt at his feet. For years she had suffered from a scourging hemorrhage; she had spent all she had on physicians, and none could cure her. She had thought that if she might but touch the hem of his garment, she would be made whole, and when she touched it, she knew she was healed.
ch32.b004: Jesus took her by the hand and lifted her up. “⟦Q 152:0.3⟧Daughter, your faith has made you whole; go in peace.⟦/Q⟧” It was her faith and not her touch that made her whole; touching the garment was merely the superstitious part of her belief. Jesus had not consciously willed this cure. He called the woman, Veronica of Caesarea-Philippi, into his presence so that neither she nor the onlookers would think that her fearful attempt to steal a cure had been honored, or that touching his garment had been effective. He wanted all to know that her pure and living faith had wrought the cure.
ch32.b006: Before they reached the ruler’s yard, a servant came out: “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Trouble not the Master; your daughter is dead.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus seemed not to heed him. Taking Peter, James, and John, he said to the grief-stricken father: “Fear not; only believe.” Inside, the flute-players and mourners were making an unseemly tumult, and when he told them the damsel was not dead, they laughed him to scorn. He put them all out of the room and went in with the father and mother and the three apostles. “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Your daughter is not dead; she is only asleep,⟦/Q⟧” he told the mother. When the house had quieted, he took the child by the hand. “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Daughter, I say to you, awake and arise!⟦/Q⟧” At once the girl rose and walked across the room, and when she had recovered from her daze, Jesus told them to give her something to eat, for she had been long without food.
ch32.b007: He explained to the family, and then to his apostles, that the maiden had been in a coma following a long fever and that he had merely aroused her, not raised her from the dead. It was futile. They were miracle-minded and lost no opportunity to ascribe another wonder to him. By this time his reputation as a healer was at its very height; everywhere he went, the sick were waiting. The Master looked much worn, and his friends began to fear he would continue to the point of collapse.
ch32.b008: The Field South of Bethsaida-Julias, Late March
ch32.b009: The crowds grew daily, and Jesus had so little rest over the Sabbath that on Sunday morning, March 27, he and the twelve slipped away across the lake, meaning to rest in a beautiful park south of Bethsaida-Julias. But the people saw the direction of the boat, hired every craft available, and followed; those who could find no boat walked around the upper end of the lake. By late afternoon more than a thousand had found him. On Monday there were more than three thousand, and by Wednesday noon about five thousand men, women, and children were gathered in the park. The weather was pleasant, for the rainy season was nearly over.
ch32.b010: By the afternoon of the third day the food the people had brought was nearly gone, yet hungry as they were, they would not leave. It was being quietly whispered that Jesus had chosen this spot, beyond the reach of Herod and the Jerusalem leaders, as the proper place to be crowned king. The enthusiasm rose every hour. Even the twelve were still tainted with such notions. Peter, John, Simon Zelotes, and Judas Iscariot favored the attempt; Andrew, James, Nathaniel, and Thomas opposed it; Matthew, Philip, and the Alpheus twins were noncommittal. The ringleader was Joab, one of the young evangelists. Not a word was said to Jesus, though of course he knew all that was going on.
ch32.b011: About five o’clock on Wednesday afternoon Jesus summoned Andrew and Philip. “⟦Q 152:2.6⟧What shall we do with the multitude? They have been with us now three days, and many of them are hungry. They have no food.⟦/Q⟧” Philip advised sending the people away to buy food in the villages, and Andrew, fearing the king plot, quickly agreed. “⟦Q 152:2.6⟧But I do not desire to send them away hungry; can you not feed them?⟦/Q⟧” Philip spoke right up: “⟦Q 152:2.6⟧Master, in this country place where can we buy bread for this multitude? Two hundred denarii worth would not be enough for lunch.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:2.7⟧Here they are, like sheep without a shepherd. I would like to feed them. What food have we with us?⟦/Q⟧” Andrew went to the Mark lad, the boy of all chores, who kept the apostles’ provisions, and came back: “⟦Q 152:2.7⟧The lad has left only five barley loaves and two dried fishes⟦/Q⟧”—and Peter promptly added, “⟦Q 152:2.7⟧We have yet to eat this evening.⟦/Q⟧”
ch32.b012: For a moment Jesus stood in silence, with a faraway look in his eyes. Then he turned to Andrew: “⟦Q 152:2.8⟧Bring me the loaves and fishes.⟦/Q⟧” He had the people sit down on the grass in companies of one hundred, each with a leader, and called all the evangelists to him. He took the loaves in his hands, gave thanks, broke the bread, and gave it to the apostles, who passed it to their associates, who carried it to the multitude; and in like manner he distributed the fishes. The multitude ate and were filled. “⟦Q 152:2.9⟧Gather up the broken pieces that remain over so that nothing will be lost,⟦/Q⟧” he said, and they gathered twelve basketfuls. This was the first and only nature miracle Jesus performed as a result of his conscious preplanning, a genuine supernatural ministration. Michael multiplied food elements as he always does, except for the elimination of the time factor and the visible life channel.
ch32.b013: The Man on the Great Stone
ch32.b014: Now the idea of making him king needed no further direction; it spread through the crowd like a contagion. The Jews had long been taught that the Messiah would make the land flow again with milk and honey, and that the bread of life would be given them as the manna was given in the wilderness. Was not all this fulfilled before their eyes? In the eyes of these simple people the power to feed carried with it the right to rule. When they had finished feasting, they rose as one man and shouted, “Make him king!”
ch32.b015: The shout had hardly ceased to echo from the rocks when Jesus stepped upon a huge stone and lifted his right hand. “⟦Q 152:3.2⟧My children, you mean well, but you are shortsighted and material-minded.⟦/Q⟧” There was a brief pause. The stalwart Galilean stood majestically in the glow of the eastern twilight, and every inch he looked a king. “⟦Q 152:3.2⟧You would make me king, not because your souls have been lighted with a great truth, but because your stomachs have been filled with bread. How many times have I told you that my kingdom is not of this world? This kingdom of heaven which we proclaim is a spiritual brotherhood, and no man rules over it seated upon a material throne.… Now all of you go hence to your own homes. If you must have a king, let the Father of lights be enthroned in the heart of each of you as the spirit Ruler of all things.⟦/Q⟧”
ch32.b016: The multitude went away stunned and disheartened, and many who had believed in him followed him no more. The apostles stood speechless around the twelve baskets of fragments. Only the Mark lad spoke: “⟦Q 152:3.3⟧And he refused to be our king.⟦/Q⟧” Before going off alone into the hills, Jesus said to Andrew: “⟦Q 152:3.3⟧Take your brethren back to Zebedee’s house and pray with them, especially for your brother, Simon Peter.⟦/Q⟧”
ch32.b018: For the first time he had sent them all away and refused to go with them. In silence the apostles rowed toward the western shore, wondering whether he had forsaken them. None was so crushed as Simon Peter. Darkness fell, and a strong contrary wind made progress almost impossible. As the hours of hard rowing passed, Peter fell into a deep sleep of exhaustion, and Andrew and James laid him on the cushioned seat in the stern.
ch32.b019: Peter dreamed that he saw Jesus coming to them walking on the sea. When the Master seemed to pass by the boat, he cried out, “Save us, Master, save us,” and those in the stern heard him. In his dream he heard Jesus say: “⟦Q 152:4.2⟧Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.⟦/Q⟧” It was like the balm of Gilead to his troubled soul. Still dreaming, he begged to come and walk with the Master on the water, but the boisterous waves frightened him, and as he began to sink he cried, “Lord, save me!” Then Jesus seemed to stretch out his hand and lift him up, saying: “⟦Q 152:4.2⟧O, you of little faith, wherefore did you doubt?⟦/Q⟧” At that moment Peter actually rose from his seat and stepped overboard, and he awoke only when Andrew, James, and John pulled him out of the sea. To Peter the experience was always real; he sincerely believed that Jesus came to them that night. But Luke, who made careful search into these matters, concluded that it was a vision of Peter’s and left it out of his narrative.
ch32.b020: They anchored near Zebedee’s house before daylight on Thursday and slept until noon. Andrew, first up, found Jesus sitting on a stone at the water’s edge with the chore boy. While many searched the eastern hills all night, he and the Mark lad had walked around the lake and back to Bethsaida after midnight. He gathered the apostles and their associates, the women included. “⟦Q 152:5.3⟧How long shall I bear with you?⟦/Q⟧” he said. “⟦Q 152:5.4⟧And now do you all see that the working of miracles and the performance of material wonders will not win souls for the spiritual kingdom? We fed the multitude, but it did not lead them to hunger for the bread of life neither to thirst for the waters of spiritual righteousness.⟦/Q⟧”
ch32.b022: They withdrew by boat to the home of a wealthy believer in the region of Gennesaret for a few days of rest, and Jesus spent much time in communion with the Father, preparing for a great crisis. Meanwhile the multitudes dispersed. In less than a month his open followers, more than fifty thousand in Galilee alone, shrank to fewer than five hundred. He wanted his apostles to learn the fickleness of popular acclaim. On the second night he told them the parable of the sower again and added: “⟦Q 152:6.3⟧You see, my children, the appeal to human feelings is transitory and utterly disappointing; the exclusive appeal to the intellect of man is likewise empty and barren; it is only by making your appeal to the spirit which lives within the human mind that you can hope to achieve lasting success.⟦/Q⟧”
ch32.b023: He warned them that the religious rulers of Jerusalem would conspire with Herod Antipas to destroy them. The twelve began to see, though not finally, that Jesus would not sit on David’s throne, and that the feeding of the five thousand and the move to make him king had been the height of the people’s miracle-seeking and of his popular acclaim. They dimly foresaw the coming times of sifting and adversity. Before they left, he told them why he had performed that extraordinary work, assuring them that he had not yielded to his sympathy for the multitude until he had ascertained that it was “according to the Father’s will.”
ch32.b024: On Sunday, April 3, Jesus set out with the twelve alone for the Passover, going by way of Gerasa and Philadelphia to avoid the crowds, and he forbade any public teaching on the journey or in Jerusalem. He entered the city only once, on the great day of the feast. The twelve learned how bitter the feeling against their Master had become, and they left Jerusalem believing that a crisis was at hand. They returned by the coast and reached Bethsaida on Friday, April 29. At once Jesus sent Andrew to ask permission to speak at the afternoon service in the Capernaum synagogue the next day. He knew well that it would be the last time he would ever be allowed to speak there.
part6: Part Six: The Time of Sifting
ch33.title: The Crisis at Capernaum
ch33.b001: April 30, A.D. 29: The Lull Before the Storm
ch33.b002: From the Friday evening of their return to Bethsaida through the Sabbath morning, the apostles could see that Jesus was seriously occupied with some momentous problem. He ate no breakfast and little at noon, and he had said hardly anything since they left Jerusalem. The twelve and their associates stood about in small groups in the house, in the garden, and along the shore, and a tension of uncertainty rested upon them all. Even Simon Peter was depressed.
ch33.b003: Nathaniel said they were in the midst of the “lull before the storm.” Thomas thought that “⟦Q 153:0.2⟧something out of the ordinary is about to happen.⟦/Q⟧” Simon Zelotes expressed the belief, in reality a hope, that “⟦Q 153:0.2⟧the Father in heaven may be about to intervene in some unexpected manner for the vindication and support of his Son,⟦/Q⟧” while Judas Iscariot dared to think that Jesus might be oppressed with regrets that “⟦Q 153:0.2⟧he did not have the courage and daring to permit the five thousand to proclaim him king of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” The only cheerful word as Jesus left the house came from one of the unsuspecting Alpheus twins: “⟦Q 153:0.3⟧We pray the Father will help you, and that we may have bigger multitudes than ever.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b004: At three o’clock on that exquisite Sabbath afternoon a distinguished congregation filled the new Capernaum synagogue. Fifty-three Pharisees and Sadducees had come down from Jerusalem, and more than thirty leaders of neighboring synagogues were present. Acting directly under orders from the Sanhedrin, they were the orthodox vanguard sent to open warfare on Jesus and his disciples. Beside them in the seats of honor sat the observers of Herod Antipas. On Friday evening and again that morning the Jerusalem leaders had pleaded with Jairus not to let Jesus speak, but his only reply was: “⟦Q 153:1.7⟧I have granted this request, and I will not violate my word.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b005: Jesus knew that he faced open warfare, and he chose boldly to take the offensive. The crisis in his own earth life had begun with the feeding of the five thousand and would end with this sermon; the crisis in the lives of the apostles began with this sermon and would last a whole year, ending only with the Master’s trial and crucifixion.
ch33.b007: He opened by reading the stern warnings of Deuteronomy, and then from Jeremiah, of how the priests and teachers sought to kill the prophet for warning them of their city’s downfall, and let him down by cords into a filthy dungeon until he sank in mire up to his armpits. “⟦Q 153:2.3⟧Today, I desire to ask you: What will the chief priests and religious leaders of this people do with the man who dares to warn them of the day of their spiritual doom?⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b008: “⟦Q 153:2.5⟧What new sign is it that you seek at my hands? I declare that you already have sufficient evidence to enable you to make your decision.… I say to you, as Joshua said to your forefathers, ‘choose you this day whom you will serve.’ Today, many of you stand at the parting of the ways.⟦/Q⟧” Some of them, he said, had hired the Tiberias fishing fleet to pursue him across the lake—not for truth, but that they might have more bread for which they had not labored. “⟦Q 153:2.7⟧My brethren, hanker not after the meat which perishes but rather seek for the spiritual food that nourishes even to eternal life.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b009: Then he pointed up to the pot of manna, embellished with grape clusters, carved on the lintel of the new synagogue. Their forefathers in the wilderness, he said, had eaten the bread of earth, not of heaven; but his Father now stood ready to give them the true bread of life. “⟦Q 153:2.8⟧I am this bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger, while he who believes me shall never thirst.⟦/Q⟧” He had come down not to do his own will but the will of him who sent him, and that will was that of all those given him he should lose not one. “⟦Q 153:2.9⟧Only yesterday did I feed you with bread for your bodies; today I offer you the bread of life for your hungry souls.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b010: A member of the Sanhedrin rose. “⟦Q 153:2.10⟧But are you not Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph, the carpenter? Are not your father and mother, as well as your brothers and sisters, well known to many of us?⟦/Q⟧” Murmuring spread, and a tumult threatened. Jesus stood up. “⟦Q 153:2.11⟧Let us be patient; the truth never suffers from honest examination. I am all that you say but more.⟦/Q⟧” The bread of life he gave, he said, was his own living and combined nature: “⟦Q 153:2.12⟧The Father in the Son and the Son one with the Father—that is my life-giving revelation to the world and my saving gift to all nations.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b011: When he finished, the ruler dismissed the congregation, but no one would leave. They crowded around him with questions while others disputed among themselves, and this went on for more than three hours.
ch33.b013: One Pharisee climbed onto a lampstand and shouted: “⟦Q 153:3.2⟧How can you give us your flesh to eat or your blood to drink?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered that he had never said his flesh was the bread of life, but that his life in the flesh was a bestowal of the bread of heaven. “⟦Q 153:3.2⟧You cannot eat my flesh nor can you drink my blood, but you can become one in spirit with me even as I am one in spirit with the Father.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b014: Then one of the Jerusalem spies objected that neither Jesus nor his apostles washed their hands properly before eating bread. To these men, eating with unwashed hands was as grave as commerce with a harlot, and both were punishable by excommunication. Jesus answered by exposing the tradition that let undutiful children declare their money “given to God” and so escape the duty of supporting their parents. “⟦Q 153:3.3⟧Why is it that you in this way make void the commandment by your own tradition?⟦/Q⟧” And he spoke to them all: “⟦Q 153:3.5⟧It is not that which enters into the mouth that spiritually defiles the man, but rather that which proceeds out of the mouth and from the heart.⟦/Q⟧” When Peter asked him to explain, he said: “⟦Q 153:3.5⟧Do you not know it is from the heart that there come forth evil thoughts, wicked projects of murder, theft, and adulteries, together with jealousy, pride, anger, revenge, railings, and false witness? And it is just such things that defile men, and not that they eat bread with ceremonially unclean hands.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b015: In the midst of the discussion a Pharisee brought forward a distraught youth possessed of an unruly and rebellious spirit. “⟦Q 153:4.1⟧What can you do for such affliction as this? Can you cast out devils?⟦/Q⟧” Moved with compassion, Jesus beckoned the lad, took him by the hand, and said: “⟦Q 153:4.1⟧You know who I am; come out of him; and I charge one of your loyal fellows to see that you do not return.⟦/Q⟧” Immediately the youth was in his right mind. This was the first case in which Jesus really cast an evil spirit out of a human being; all the earlier cases had been only supposed possession.
ch33.b016: At once a Pharisee charged that Jesus was in league with devils and did all his works by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of devils. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 153:4.3⟧How can Satan cast out Satan? A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand; if a house be divided against itself, it is soon brought to desolation.⟦/Q⟧” He gave a solemn warning to any who, with open eyes and premeditated malice, would ascribe the works of God to devils, for such persistent workers of iniquity would never seek nor receive forgiveness. When another Pharisee demanded a predetermined sign, he answered: “⟦Q 153:4.5⟧This faithless and sign-seeking generation seeks a token, but no sign shall be given you other than that which you already have, and that which you shall see when the Son of Man departs from among you.⟦/Q⟧” It was well past seven when the apostles surrounded him and led him out. In silence they walked home to Bethsaida, amazed and somewhat terror-stricken. They had never seen him act in so militant a manner.
ch33.b018: At home Jesus refused to eat and isolated himself for hours in an upper room. The desertion of the populace had been sudden and complete. Almost at midnight Joab, the leader of the evangelists, came in to report that about a third of his associates had deserted the cause. All evening loyal disciples brought word that feeling throughout Capernaum had turned against the Master. At Peter’s house the twelve women met, tremendously upset, but none of them deserted.
ch33.b019: A little after midnight Jesus came down and stood among the twelve and their associates, about thirty in all. “⟦Q 153:5.3⟧I recognize that this sifting of the kingdom distresses you, but it is unavoidable.… Why do you grieve when the new day is dawning for the shining forth in new glory of the spiritual teachings of the kingdom of heaven?⟦/Q⟧” And he went on: “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧My beloved, you must remember that it is the spirit that quickens; the flesh and all that pertains thereto is of little profit. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Be of good cheer! I have not deserted you.⟦/Q⟧” Then he asked whether they too would desert him at such a time, and warned that one of them stood in grave danger. Simon Peter answered: “⟦Q 153:5.4⟧Yes, Lord, we are sad and perplexed, but we will never forsake you. You have taught us the words of eternal life.⟦/Q⟧” With one accord the others nodded. “Go to your rest,” said Jesus, “⟦Q 153:5.5⟧for busy times are upon us; active days are just ahead.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b020: That same night, at Tiberias, commissioners of the Sanhedrin urged Herod Antipas to arrest Jesus. But Chuza, whose wife Joanna belonged to the women’s corps, had told Herod that Jesus had no intention of meddling in earthly rule, and Herod, haunted by a bad conscience over the death of John the Baptist, wanted no part in the intrigue. When the Jews threatened to report to Caesar that he was shielding a traitor, he ordered them out of his council chamber.
ch33.b022: From May 1 to May 7 Jesus held counsel morning, afternoon, and evening at the Zebedee house with about a hundred disciples who had the moral courage to declare openly for him. On Friday the rulers of the Capernaum synagogue closed it to Jesus and all his followers. Jairus resigned as chief ruler and openly took his stand with Jesus. At the last seaside meeting, on Sabbath afternoon, May 7, fewer than one hundred and fifty listened. That night marked the lowest ebb of popular regard for Jesus. From then on there was a slow but healthier growth of a new following, better grounded in spiritual faith.
ch33.b023: On Sunday, May 8, the Sanhedrin passed an unprecedented decree closing all the synagogues of Palestine to Jesus and his followers. Five of its members resigned in protest, and within two weeks every synagogue had bowed except Hebron, whose rulers insisted on their congregational autonomy. That same morning Jesus declared a week’s holiday: “⟦Q 154:2.2⟧Go to your several places to play or fish while you pray for the extension of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” He visited many families about the seaside and went fishing several times with David Zebedee; wherever he walked alone, two or three of David’s most trusted messengers lurked nearby to guard him. That week Nathaniel and James Zebedee were acutely ill for three days and nights, and on the third night Jesus sent Salome to rest and himself ministered to them. He could have healed them instantly, but never once in his life in the flesh did he engage in supernatural ministry for his own family or his immediate followers.
ch33.b024: On May 18 Herod agreed that the Sanhedrin authorities might seize Jesus if the Roman ruler of Judea concurred. On Saturday night, May 21, word came that the civil authorities at Jerusalem had no objection, and just before midnight Herod signed the decree, though he well knew Jesus could not expect a fair trial from his bitter enemies. In Capernaum that same night fifty leading citizens debated past midnight, “⟦Q 154:4.1⟧What shall we do with Jesus?⟦/Q⟧”—and could find no agreement.
ch33.b026: Before daybreak on Sunday one of David’s messengers arrived in haste from Tiberias with word that the arrest had been authorized. David roused his messengers and summoned all the disciples to an emergency council at seven o’clock. Jesus bade them farewell for the time being and directed them to carry on the work of the kingdom regardless of consequences. He chose twelve of the evangelists to go with him, told the twelve apostles to remain with him whatever happened, and instructed the twelve women to stay at the Zebedee and Peter houses until he sent for them. “⟦Q 154:5.3⟧My men will never lose contact with you,⟦/Q⟧” David promised. About seven-thirty Jesus began his parting address to nearly a hundred believers crowded indoors. The seriousness of weeks had gone, and he was unusually cheerful, once more his normal self.
ch33.b027: About eight o’clock five members of his family arrived—Mary, James, Joseph, Jude, and Ruth—summoned by Jude’s sister-in-law. They had spent the previous evening with the Pharisees, who labored to persuade Mary that her son was beside himself. “⟦Q 154:6.2⟧I know I could influence my son if he would only come home and listen to me,⟦/Q⟧” Mary said. Of all the family only Ruth believed wholeheartedly in his mission, and to all of this she would say only: “⟦Q 154:6.3⟧I will tell my brother that I think he is a man of God.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b028: The house was crowded to overflowing, so they stood on the back porch and passed word in from person to person, until Simon Peter interrupted the Master to whisper: “⟦Q 154:6.4⟧Behold, your mother and your brothers are outside, and they are very anxious to speak with you.⟦/Q⟧” Mary expected him to come out at once. She did not know how important this parting message was, nor that his apprehenders might arrive at any moment. Instead they heard his musical voice speak with increased volume: “⟦Q 154:6.5⟧Say to my mother and my brothers that they should have no fear for me. The Father who sent me into the world will not forsake me; neither shall any harm come upon my family.… For whosoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, the same is my mother, my brother, and my sister.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b029: When Mary heard these words, she collapsed in Jude’s arms, and they carried her into the garden. Jesus intended to finish his address and then visit with his family, not wishing their first meeting after so long a separation to be so public an affair. But a messenger arrived from Tiberias: the officers of the Sanhedrin were on their way. Just then a woman in the room stood up and exclaimed, “⟦Q 154:6.7⟧Blessed is the womb that bore you and blessed are the breasts that nursed you.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus turned to her: “⟦Q 154:6.7⟧No, rather is the one blessed who hears the word of God and dares to obey it.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus did not forsake his earth family; they forsook him. In later years, when James had joined the early Christian movement, he suffered immeasurably for having missed this time with his brother.
ch33.b031: At that moment a party of David’s messengers burst in at the rear entrance, and the apostles, thinking them the arresting officers, hurried the Master out the front door to the waiting boat. That is why Jesus never saw his family waiting on the back porch. As he stepped into the boat, he said to David: “⟦Q 154:6.12⟧Tell my mother and my brothers that I appreciate their coming, and that I intended to see them. Admonish them to find no offense in me but rather to seek for a knowledge of the will of God and for grace and courage to do that will.⟦/Q⟧”
ch33.b032: It was almost half past eight on this beautiful Sunday morning, May 22, A.D. 29, when the company of twenty-five—Jesus, the twelve apostles, and the twelve evangelists—manned the oars and pulled for the eastern shore. A smaller boat with six of David’s messengers followed. The crowd lingered about the Zebedee house watching the two boats, and they were well out on the lake when the Jerusalem officers hurried up. Refusing to believe he had escaped, they spent almost a week searching vainly around Capernaum.
ch33.b033: Jesus never again made his home at the house of Zebedee. From now on, through the rest of his earth life, the Master truly “⟦Q 154:7.2⟧had not where to lay his head.⟦/Q⟧” His family went back to their home in Capernaum, confused and full of consternation, and found no peace of mind until Thursday afternoon, when Ruth learned from David that her father-brother was safe and making his way toward the Phoenician coast.
ch34.title: Flight to Gentile Lands
ch34.b001: The Same Field Again, May A.D. 29
ch34.b002: Soon after landing near Kheresa on that eventful Sunday, Jesus and the twenty-four walked a little way north and spent the night in the beautiful park south of Bethsaida-Julias—the very place where, two months before, five thousand had sat on the grass and eaten. Before they lay down to sleep, the Master gathered them about him to discuss plans for a tour through Batanea and northern Galilee to the Phoenician coast, and he recalled the words of the Psalmist: “⟦Q 155:1.1⟧Why do the heathen rage and the peoples plot in vain?⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b003: “⟦Q 155:1.2⟧Today you see this fulfilled before your eyes,⟦/Q⟧” he said. But they would not see the rest of the psalm fulfilled, with its talk of breaking the nations with a rod of iron. “⟦Q 155:1.2⟧My kingdom is founded on love, proclaimed in mercy, and established by unselfish service.⟦/Q⟧” He would receive the so-called heathen, in reality his untaught brethren, with open arms of mercy. And the heathen, he added, were not without excuse when they raged: “⟦Q 155:1.3⟧Because their outlook is small and narrow, they are able to concentrate their energies enthusiastically.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles, by contrast, were too vacillating. “⟦Q 155:1.3⟧You are hardly worthy of the kingdom when your service consists so largely in an attitude of regretting the past, whining over the present, and vainly hoping for the future.… Cease your useless yearning and go forth bravely doing that which concerns the establishment of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” And he told them: “⟦Q 155:1.5⟧If you, by truth co-ordination, learn to exemplify in your lives this beautiful wholeness of righteousness, your fellow men will then seek after you that they may gain what you have so acquired.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b005: On Monday morning, May 23, Jesus sent Peter with the twelve evangelists to Chorazin, while he and the eleven went up the Jordan and northeast to Caesarea-Philippi. The two weeks at Chorazin were a veritable baptism of adversity for the evangelists. No city of all Galilee yielded so few souls for the kingdom. Following Peter’s instructions, they said less about healing and preached the spiritual truths of the kingdom with increased vigor. Deprived of the satisfaction of winning souls, each man took stock more earnestly of his own soul and its progress. On June 8 they joined the Master at Caesarea-Philippi, and that evening, hearing of their experiences, Jesus spoke again of the parable of the sower and of the meaning of the apparent failure of life undertakings.
ch34.b006: The weeks near Caesarea-Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, were a real test for the eleven as well. There was no public work, they missed the stimulation of Peter’s enthusiasm, and they were well-nigh depressed. Yet in their daily talks with the Master they learned much. They learned that when truth becomes formulated as a boundary line of self-righteous exclusiveness instead of serving as a signpost of spiritual progress, it loses its life-giving power and becomes merely fossilizing. They learned that many souls can best be led to love the unseen God by first being taught to love the brethren they can see, and that true religion is man’s heartfelt loyalty to his highest and truest convictions. Jesus warned them that, if their religious longings were only material, increasing knowledge of nature would in time deprive them of their faith in God; but if their religion were spiritual, never could the progress of physical science disturb their faith in eternal realities.
ch34.b008: On Thursday morning, June 9, after David’s messengers brought word of the progress of the kingdom, the twenty-five set out for the Phoenician coast. Near Luz they paused for lunch in the shadow of an overhanging ledge of rock, and no sooner had they sat down than Peter asked: “⟦Q 155:4.2⟧Master, since the Father in heaven knows all things, and since his spirit is our support in the establishment of the kingdom of heaven on earth, why is it that we flee from the threats of our enemies?⟦/Q⟧” Before Jesus could answer, Thomas broke in: “⟦Q 155:4.2⟧What is the real difference between their religion and ours? Why is it we are at such diversity of belief when we all profess to serve the same God?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said that it would help them all more if he answered Thomas, and that he would do so when they had finished their lunch.
ch34.b009: Then, there under the rock, he gave one of the most remarkable addresses the apostles ever heard. There are, he said, three forms of religious devotion found among every people: primitive religion, the instinctive fear of mysterious energies; the religion of civilization, the religion of the mind, resting on the authority of established tradition; and true religion, the religion of the spirit as demonstrated in human experience. The religions of authority offer a ready refuge to which the distraught soul may flee when harassed by fear and tormented by uncertainty, and they ask in return only a passive, intellectual assent. But the religion of the spirit means effort, struggle, conflict, faith, determination, love, loyalty, and progress. It is the supreme adventure of all human existence—man seeking God, for himself and as himself, and finding him.
ch34.b010: “At Jerusalem,” Jesus said, “⟦Q 155:5.12⟧the religious leaders have formulated the various doctrines of their traditional teachers and the prophets of other days into an established system of intellectual beliefs, a religion of authority.… And now are we about to enter upon a deadly conflict with such a religion.⟦/Q⟧” Then, pointing to each of the twenty-four and calling him by name, he asked: “⟦Q 155:5.13⟧And now, which one of you would prefer to take this easy path of conformity to an established and fossilized religion, as defended by the Pharisees at Jerusalem.… Are you fearful, soft, and ease-seeking? Are you afraid to trust your future in the hands of the God of truth, whose sons you are?⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b011: All twenty-four sprang to their feet to pledge their loyalty, for this was one of the few emotional appeals Jesus ever made to them. But he raised his hand and stopped them. “⟦Q 155:5.14⟧Go now apart by yourselves, each man alone with the Father, and there find the unemotional answer to my question.⟦/Q⟧” They scattered among the rocks for a short time, their spirits uplifted and their emotions mightily stirred. When Andrew called them together, the Master said only: “Let us resume our journey.” For a while they walked in silence. Then they began to talk among themselves, and by three o’clock that afternoon they could go no farther. They halted, and Peter came to Jesus: “⟦Q 155:5.16⟧Master, you have spoken to us the words of life and truth. We would hear more; we beseech you to speak to us further concerning these matters.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b012: In the Shade of the Hillside
ch34.b013: So, in the shade of the hillside, Jesus went on teaching them about the religion of the spirit. They had dared, he said in substance, to reject the authority of the traditions of record now regarded as the word of God. The Father had indeed spoken through Moses, Elijah, Isaiah, Amos, and Hosea, but he did not cease to minister words of truth when those prophets made an end of speaking. They must not commit the folly of calling divine that which is wholly human, nor fail to discern words of truth that come through no traditional oracle. He admonished them to give up always quoting the prophets of old and praising the heroes of Israel, and instead to become living prophets of the Most High themselves.
ch34.b014: The religions of authority, he said, can only divide men and set them against each other, for they require uniformity of belief. The religion of the spirit requires only unity of experience, making full allowance for diversity of belief, and it alone can draw mankind into brotherhood. Yet they must not look with disdain upon the children of Abraham, fallen on days of traditional barrenness; for weary generations, from Moses to Amos and Hosea, Israel had toiled and sweated and groaned to come a little nearer the truth about God, and so had prepared the way for the greater revelation they were called to share.
ch34.b015: He reminded them that the will of God can be done in any earthly occupation; some callings are not holy and others secular, for all things are sacred in the lives of those who are spirit led. And they need not try to prove to other men that they had found God. There were only two demonstrations of it: the fruits of the spirit showing forth in their daily lives, and an entire life plan that risked everything they were and had on the adventure of finding the God of eternity. When he had finished, he beckoned to Andrew and, pointing west toward Phoenicia, said: “⟦Q 155:6.19⟧Let us be on our way.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b017: On Friday afternoon, June 10, they reached the outskirts of Sidon and stopped at the home of Karuska, a well-to-do woman who had been a patient in the Bethsaida hospital. Jesus asked his associates to tell no one he was there, for he wished to rest. But Karuska’s servant told a Syrian neighbor named Norana, whose daughter of about twelve suffered from a grievous nervous disorder with convulsions. The mother believed that her child was possessed by an unclean spirit.
ch34.b018: On the Sabbath afternoon Norana came with her daughter. The Alpheus twins explained that the Master was resting, and she answered that she would wait right there. Peter reasoned with her in vain: “⟦Q 156:1.3⟧I will not depart until I have seen your Master.⟦/Q⟧” Thomas tried to send her away, and she asked him: “⟦Q 156:1.4⟧What has happened to you, his disciples, that you would send away those who come seeking your Master’s help?⟦/Q⟧” Then Simon Zelotes said: “⟦Q 156:1.5⟧Woman, you are a Greek-speaking gentile. It is not right that you should expect the Master to take the bread intended for the children of the favored household and cast it to the dogs.⟦/Q⟧” Norana refused to take offense. “⟦Q 156:1.5⟧Yes, teacher, I understand your words. I am only a dog in the eyes of the Jews, but as concerns your Master, I am a believing dog.… And even you, my good man, would not dare to deprive the dogs of the privilege of obtaining the crumbs which chance to fall from the children’s table.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b019: Just then the girl was seized with a violent convulsion before them all, and her mother cried out that they were not worthy to be his disciples. Jesus had heard everything through an open window. To their surprise he came outside. “⟦Q 156:1.7⟧O woman, great is your faith, so great that I cannot withhold that which you desire; go your way in peace. Your daughter already has been made whole.⟦/Q⟧” The girl was well from that hour. It was not only Norana’s great and persistent faith but also her sense of humor that touched the Master’s heart. “⟦Q 156:2.8⟧My people take themselves too seriously,⟦/Q⟧” he once said to Thomas; “⟦Q 156:2.8⟧they are just about devoid of an appreciation of humor.⟦/Q⟧” The next day he told the apostles: “⟦Q 156:1.8⟧Verily, verily, I tell you that the Father’s kingdom shall be taken by the gentiles if the children of Abraham are not minded to show faith enough to enter therein.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b021: As they entered Sidon, they crossed a bridge, the first many of them had ever seen, and Jesus said: “⟦Q 156:2.1⟧This world is only a bridge; you may pass over it, but you should not think to build a dwelling place upon it.⟦/Q⟧” He stayed just north of the city in the home of Justa and her mother, Bernice, teaching the twenty-four each morning while they went out to preach in the afternoons and evenings. The Greek-speaking Syrophoenicians received the gospel warmly. Many of them came to know not only that Jesus was like God but also that God was like Jesus. They were not afraid of him; they dared to accept his message. It was in Justa’s house that he first told his disciples that “⟦Q 156:2.5⟧even though heaven and earth shall pass away, my words of truth shall not.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b022: At the end of June they went up the coast to Porphyreon and Heldua, while Jesus visited Beirut alone for a few days. From July 11 to July 24 they worked in Tyre. Two by two, each apostle with an evangelist, they crossed daily into the busy seaport by way of Alexander’s mole, and its polyglot people heard them gladly. Even the doors of the Melkarth temple were opened to Jesus. Many of the makers of Tyrian purple believed, and when the shellfish that yielded their dye began to fail, they migrated to the ends of the earth in search of new habitats, carrying with them the gospel of the kingdom.
ch34.b023: Jesus spoke publicly in Tyre only once, on the afternoon of July 20. He told them of the white lily that rears its pure and snowy head high into the sunshine while its roots are grounded in the slime and muck of the darkened soil. “Likewise,” said he, “⟦Q 156:5.1⟧mortal man, while he has his roots of origin and being in the animal soil of human nature, can by faith raise his spiritual nature up into the sunlight of heavenly truth and actually bear the noble fruits of the spirit.⟦/Q⟧” In the same sermon he used his first and only parable drawn from his own trade, warning them not to be like “⟦Q 156:5.2⟧the foolish carpenter who wastes valuable time squaring, measuring, and smoothing his worm-eaten and inwardly rotting timber,⟦/Q⟧” only to reject it at last as unfit for the foundation.
ch34.b024: That evening Nathaniel asked why they prayed not to be led into temptation, when the Father never does such things. Jesus explained that their forefathers had seen the hand of God in everything, good and evil alike, but that men are all too often led into temptation by their own selfishness and animal impulses. He warned against trying to overcome temptation by the mere force of will. “⟦Q 156:5.5⟧The old and the inferior will be forgotten in the love for the new and the superior.… And again I say to you, be not overcome by evil but rather overcome evil with good.⟦/Q⟧”
ch34.b025: Back to the Sea of Galilee, August A.D. 29
ch34.b026: The day before leaving Tyre, Jesus sent the twelve evangelists home by a different route, and they were never again so intimately associated with him. On July 24 he and the twelve went down the coast to Ptolemais and then inland by Jotapata, Ramah, and Zebulun to Gennesaret, where they met David Zebedee. That same evening a boat took them across toward Kheresa, and after a day in the hills they rested three days in the park where the five thousand had been fed. About fifty men and women came to them there—the remnant of the once numerous believers of Capernaum.
ch34.b027: While Jesus was away, his enemies had concluded that the movement was broken and that he was too frightened ever to return, and active opposition had all but subsided. The order closing the synagogues had turned the people against the Pharisees, and many rulers began quietly to open their synagogues to Abner and his associates. Philip, Herod’s brother, had become a halfhearted believer and sent word that the Master was free to live and work in his domains. Even Herod Antipas let it be known that, though he had signed warrants for Jesus’ arrest in Galilee, he had not authorized it in Perea.
ch34.b028: Such was the situation about the first of August, A.D. 29, when the Master returned from Phoenicia and began to reorganize his scattered, tested, and depleted forces for the last eventful year of his mission on earth. The issues of battle were now clearly drawn, as he and his associates prepared to proclaim the religion of the spirit of the living God who dwells in the minds of men.
